lessons.title: Chat, SMS, WhatsApp, and the idle-chat quota
lessons.why: A chat that has gone quiet is still an active chat. The default ceiling is 500, shared with SMS, WhatsApp, and Apple Messages for Business.
paras: Connect Customer prices a chat message at 0.010 USD sent or received, and the worked example includes manager questions and AI replies as messages. SMS and third-party messaging are 0.014 USD per message before the provider's delivery fee. Basic prices are lower and listed separately.
Persistent chat is the documented way to avoid counting a long silence against the quota. Widget origins must be allowed or the browser will not start the session.
points: StartChatContact is an API. Call it from your backend.
The same queue and routing profile can include chat with its own concurrency.
Attachments and rich messages have size limits. Email attachments are a different channel.
Alarm on concurrent chats at 80 percent.
lessons.mistake: Load-testing the widget from a laptop and calling that capacity planning.

lessons.title: Email is a contact with a 90-day thread
lessons.why: An email is not a chat transcript and not a case, though it can create both.
paras: Connect Customer lists 0.080 USD per email. Basic lists 0.050 USD plus a small delivery fee in the example. Threads stay together for 90 days. Active email contacts expire at 14 days unless you set connect:ContactExpiry, and never beyond 90. The concurrent active email quota defaults to 1000.
One Connect email domain and up to 100 custom domains. Fifty addresses across To and Cc. No BCC.
points: Outbound email from an agent and a flow acknowledgment are both billable messages in the examples.
SES networking applies if you send a lot.
Put the case id in the thread so the next reply finds it.
Do not staff email on a voice-only routing profile.
lessons.mistake: Treating a reply on day 91 as the same contact. It is a new thread.

lessons.title: Campaigns dial only after the quota is not zero
lessons.why: The default concurrent campaign call quota is 0. The symptom is a fast busy, and it is not a carrier outage.
paras: You get 50 active campaigns and 500 total per instance as defaults. Voice minutes on a campaign are priced higher than ordinary voice. Check call progress is the answering-machine branch and it only works in campaign flows.
A campaign needs a caller ID you are allowed to present, a calling window, and agents or an agentless flow that can actually finish the conversation.
points: Raise the concurrent campaign quota before the first run.
AMD branches need a prompt for humans and a disposition for machines.
Compliance with calling hours is your job. The block will dial when the campaign says to.
Email and SMS campaigns use the message prices, not the voice minute.
lessons.mistake: Pointing a campaign at a queue that nobody is staffed for, then blaming AMD.

lessons.title: In-app, web, and video
lessons.why: The customer does not dial. The widget starts a contact. You still pay for voice minutes plus the media type.
paras: In-app and web audio is 0.010 USD per minute on top of the voice service charge. Video is 0.015 USD per minute per participant. Screen sharing is 0.015 USD per minute. The customer's widget and the agent's workstation have different network requirements. Video adds *.chime.aws and does not support VDI.
The flow is still a flow. Attributes still matter. The difference is the endpoint.
points: Test the customer network, not only the agent's.
A video failure with working audio is a Chime path problem.
Record the fact that video was used. It changes the price and the privacy notice.
lessons.mistake: Assuming the CCP allow list covers the customer's browser.

number.n: Per minute, on top of voice

diagram.caption: Both must pass media. They are not the same firewall.
